passage:
Supervisor's note, internship programme, week 6. Hrithik

Tejas had a brilliant Monday: the client loved the prototype and the whole team cheered. By Tuesday evening Tejas had volunteered for the weekend hackathon, offered to redo the onboarding slides, agreed to mentor two first-years, and planned to cycle to the office on the flooded route "because it'll be fine".
I asked how the college assignments due Friday fit in. A long pause. "Oh. I forgot those."
Nothing is wrong with enthusiasm, and the good mood was earned. But the yeses came faster than the checking.
What I did next: sat with Tejas and listed every commitment with its hours. Tejas dropped the slides and the hackathon, kept one mentee, and took the bus. We agreed on a rule: sleep on any new yes.

qa.q: How many first-years did Tejas agree to mentor?
qa.a: Two first-years.

qa.q: Why did the flooded cycle route seem fine to Tejas?
qa.a: After the client loved the prototype, Tejas felt on top of the world, and that glow made risks look small and every yes feel easy.

qa.q: What rule did they agree on, and why does it help?
qa.a: Sleep on any new yes; a night's pause lets the checking catch up with the good mood.

qa.q: How does Hrithik view Tejas's burst of yeses?
qa.a: Hrithik sees the enthusiasm as earned and welcome, but worries the commitments outran the checking, especially with assignments due Friday.

grounding: A supervisor records how an intern's great mood led to too many yeses and a risky commute, and how they slowed down together.

passage:
Friday night!! 🎉

Best day of the year. Got the lead in the college play AND my scholarship renewal came through. I felt like I could fly.

So when Hemant asked if I'd drive his dad's car to the lake at midnight with the whole gang, I said yes before he finished. Also said yes to the fest committee, to tutoring Hemant's cousin every morning, and to a Sunday trek that's supposed to be "moderate" (it isn't, I checked later).

Just looked at my calendar. Rehearsals start Monday. Quiz on Tuesday. I've driven at night exactly once, on a practice round, and it was scary.

Why did all of it sound so easy at 5 p.m.? Everything looked shiny.

Tomorrow: tell Hemant I'm not driving. Keep the play, keep the committee. The rest can wait.
Raghav

qa.q: What two pieces of good news did Raghav get?
qa.a: The lead in the college play and the scholarship renewal.

qa.q: Why did the midnight drive sound easy to Raghav at 5 p.m.?
qa.a: The joy of the day made everything look shiny, so a night drive felt like fun rather than a risk for someone who had driven at night only once. 😅

qa.q: Which of Raghav's plans for tomorrow is wisest, and why?
qa.a: Telling Hemant no to the night drive, because it is the riskiest yes; keeping only the play and the committee also protects rehearsals and the quiz.

qa.q: How might Hemant react when Raghav backs out of driving?
qa.a: Hemant might be disappointed at first, but could also be relieved that his dad's car won't be driven at night by someone so new to it.

grounding: A student on a joyful day says yes to a risky night drive and too many plans, then sees the risks once the glow fades.

passage: The morning Ramesh, twenty, heard he was picked for the district kabaddi team, the whole of Saoner seemed to sparkle. By noon he'd said yes to everything. Yes, he'd fix Kaka's tractor tonight. Yes, he'd lead the temple fair volunteers tomorrow. Yes, he'd ride his cousin's old motorbike to Nagpur after dark to fetch sweets, never mind the bald front tyre and the drizzle. "Nothing can go wrong today," he told his sister Yamini, grinning. "The tyre?" she asked. "It's fine, it's fine." The bike skidded on the wet turn by the dhaba; he got away with a torn trouser and a scraped palm. He got home at midnight, left the tractor half-done, and overslept practice. At breakfast Yamini put a plaster on his palm. "Big day yesterday," she said. He winced. "Too big.

qa.q: What was wrong with the cousin's motorbike?
qa.a: It had a bald front tyre, and it was drizzling.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh brush off the tyre and the drizzle?
qa.a: His happy mood made everything feel safe and easy, so risks that he would normally notice didn't seem to matter that day.

qa.q: What could Ramesh do the next time big good news makes him want to say yes to everything?
qa.a: He could pause before agreeing, pick one or two things, and check risks like a bald tyre as if it were an ordinary day.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt watching her brother agree to everything?
qa.a: She seemed worried, asking about the tyre, and later relieved but a little dry when she plastered his palm.

grounding: A young man in a great mood after good news underestimates risks and takes on too much.

passage: Tariq got the email at 4 p.m. on Friday: the summer internship in Toronto was his. He danced around the flat. Within an hour, he'd said yes to three things. Yes, he'd cover a double shift at the bookshop on Saturday. Yes, he'd host his cousins for dinner Saturday night. And when his flatmate Liam mentioned the ridge trail on Sunday, still iced over and marked closed, Tariq laughed. "We'll be fine, we'll be careful." Liam looked at him. "You'd never say that normally." Tariq shrugged. "Today's not normal." By Saturday midnight, after the double shift and the dishes, he was so tired he could barely stand. On Sunday morning, reading the trail warning again, he felt his stomach drop. "I think I said yes to all this because I was so happy," he texted Liam. "Can we do the lake walk instead?"

qa.q: What was wrong with the ridge trail on Sunday?
qa.a: It was still iced over and marked closed.

qa.q: Why did the closed trail seem fine to Tariq on Friday?
qa.a: His joy about the internship made risks feel small and everything seem possible, so the warning didn't sink in.

qa.q: What did Tariq do on Sunday morning that was wise?
qa.a: He reread the warning in a calmer state, saw his mood had pushed his choices, and suggested the safer lake walk instead.

qa.q: How might Liam have felt when Tariq said, "Today's not normal"?
qa.a: Liam seemed uneasy, noticing that Tariq was ignoring risks Tariq usually respected, and perhaps unsure how to push back.

grounding: A young adult in a joyful mood underestimates a risk and says yes to too much, then sees it the next day.

passage:
Diary, 11 p.m.

I GOT THE INTERNSHIP. Madhuri from Room 14, summer analyst, actual stipend. I screamed in the corridor.

Then, in one afternoon, I said yes to:
- running the cultural fest decoration team (they asked, I was glowing, why not?)
- tutoring Bhupen's cousin for board maths, three evenings a week
- the Himachal trek in May, even though the internship starts in May
- rewriting the club newsletter by Sunday

It all felt easy. Like I had extra hours hidden somewhere. Bhupen asked, "Are you sure about the trek dates?" and I laughed and said I'd manage.

Now I'm looking at the calendar and May has two of me in it. Also mid-sems are next week, which I forgot existed.

Tomorrow, when I'm less buzzy, I'll go through this list again. Some of these yeses need to become "actually, sorry."

qa.q: What was the first thing Madhuri said yes to after the internship news?
qa.a: Running the cultural fest decoration team.

qa.q: Why did all those yeses feel easy to Madhuri at the time?
qa.a: Madhuri was thrilled and glowing about the internship, and that happy mood made every task seem light and every clash look manageable.

qa.q: What could Madhuri do tomorrow to fix the overload?
qa.a: Madhuri could check each yes against the calendar and the mid-sems, keep the ones that fit, and politely withdraw from the clashing ones soon.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Madhuri's quick yes to the trek?
qa.a: Bhupen seems doubtful and a little concerned, since Bhupen noticed the date clash and got only a laugh in return.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a joyful mood underestimating risks and clashes and agreeing to far too many commitments.

passage: The results came the morning of the village fair near Thanjavur: Kavitha had topped her college. By noon she was floating. She told her aunt Usha she would cook for the whole family's pooja tomorrow, all forty people. She promised the headmaster she'd teach the evening class for the fair week. When her cousins said the last bus back to college left at ten tonight and was often empty, she said, "I'll take it, no problem, I'm not scared of anything today." Usha watched her over the sweet stall. "Kavitha, your practical is tomorrow morning. And the pooja is also tomorrow." Kavitha laughed, then stopped. "Oh." Usha squeezed her arm. "Be happy. Then decide with a cup of tea." Kavitha asked her uncle to ride with her to the bus stand, and gave the pooja to her cousins.

qa.q: What did Kavitha promise the headmaster?
qa.a: She promised to teach the evening class for the fair week.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha feel she could do everything that day?
qa.a: She was delighted and proud after topping her college, and the joy made risks like the late empty bus and the clashing dates seem tiny.

qa.q: What small step did Usha suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Usha suggested deciding over a cup of tea, which gives the happy mood time to settle so Kavitha can check dates and risks clearly.

qa.q: How might Usha see Kavitha's promises at the fair?
qa.a: Usha seems fond and proud but also concerned, noticing the clashes and the late bus that Kavitha's high spirits were hiding.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose great mood makes risks look small and leads her to promise too much until an elder helps her pause.

passage:
Jana, twenty, had just passed her driving test in Berlin and got an A on her history paper the same week. She felt unstoppable.

When her friend Layla asked her to help organise a birthday party, she said yes. When her boss asked her to cover two extra shifts, she said yes. When a classmate suggested a road trip that weekend, she said yes to that too.

"You're doing all three?" Layla asked.

"Easy," Jana said, grinning. "I'll make it work."

By Saturday, she was exhausted, late for the party, and cancelled on the road trip at the last minute. Sitting on the tram, she wondered how everything had seemed so easy on Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Jana pass that week?
qa.a: Her driving test.

qa.q: Why did Jana say yes to everything?
qa.a: She felt joyful and unstoppable after her successes, so every plan seemed easy and the risks seemed small.

qa.q: What could Jana do next time she's in a great mood and gets asked for things?
qa.a: She could say "let me check and get back to you" and look at her schedule before agreeing.

qa.q: How might Layla feel when Jana is late for the party?
qa.a: Layla might feel disappointed and a bit frustrated, since Jana had said it would be easy.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood underestimates risks and says yes to too much.

passage:
At the college sports club, Madhav, nineteen, had just won the inter-college badminton final. He was glowing.

The coach, Kishore sir, came over. "Madhav, would you like to lead the junior training on weekends?"

"Yes! Definitely!"

A classmate asked him to join a hackathon. "Sure, count me in!"

Another friend asked about a night trek on the same weekend. "Absolutely!"

That evening, Kishore sir stopped him. "Madhav, you just agreed to three things on the same Saturday."

Madhav blinked. It hadn't seemed like a problem an hour ago. Everything had felt possible.

"When you're this happy, everything looks easy," the coach said. "Sleep on it and tell me tomorrow."

qa.q: What had Madhav just won?
qa.a: The inter-college badminton final.

qa.q: Why didn't Madhav notice the clash at first?
qa.a: He was so happy and excited after winning that everything felt possible and he didn't see the risks.

qa.q: What did Kishore sir suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He suggested sleeping on it, so Madhav could decide once his joy had settled and see the clashes clearly.

qa.q: How might the classmate who invited Madhav to the hackathon feel if he pulled out?
qa.a: The classmate might feel let down, especially if they had counted on him.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood underestimates risks and says yes to too much.

passage:
Dear Gargi,

Remember when I got that internship offer in May? I was so happy I agreed to everything that week: helping Chachu shift houses, a trip to Rishikesh, and a part-time tutoring job.

I didn't even check dates. Everything felt doable. I thought, I'm on a roll, what could go wrong?

Then all three landed on the same fortnight. I let Chachu down, cancelled the trip, and nearly lost the tutoring job. The internship started and I was already tired.

I'm writing because you've just got your scholarship, and you sound over the moon. Please enjoy it. But before you say yes to anything, sleep on it.

Irfan

qa.q: What three things did Irfan agree to that week?
qa.a: Helping Chachu shift houses, a trip to Rishikesh and a part-time tutoring job.

qa.q: Why did everything feel doable to Irfan in May?
qa.a: Irfan felt joyful and on a roll after the internship offer, so problems seemed unlikely.

qa.q: What advice does Irfan give Gargi, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Sleep on it before saying yes, because a very happy mood can make risks and clashes seem small.

qa.q: How might Chachu have felt when Irfan let him down?
qa.a: Chachu probably felt disappointed and let down, having counted on help with the move.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood says yes to too much, underestimating clashes and risks.

passage: Karthik, you asked how I ended up with four commitments in one week? Okay. It was the day I got the internship offer. I was flying. Wasim the unstoppable, right? So when the fest team asked me to run the stall, I said yes. When my cousin asked for help shifting his flat on Saturday, yes. When our professor needed a volunteer for the conference, yes, obviously. And that bike trip to the hills with you lot on Sunday? Yes, even though my bike needs new brakes. In that mood nothing looked hard or risky. It all looked fun! Then Thursday came. I was exhausted, and I realised I'd forgotten my own assignment. So I've cancelled the bike trip, sorry, and I'm getting the brakes fixed first.

qa.q: What was wrong with Wasim's bike?
qa.a: It needed new brakes.

qa.q: Why did Wasim say yes to everything that day?
qa.a: Wasim felt elated and unstoppable after the internship offer, so every task looked fun and nothing looked risky.

qa.q: What could Wasim try the next time good news arrives?
qa.a: Wait a day before saying yes to new commitments, and weigh each one, especially risks like the brakes, when calmer.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel about the cancelled bike trip?
qa.a: Karthik may be disappointed but relieved too, since riding with bad brakes was a real danger that Wasim's mood had hidden.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood says yes to too much and overlooks a real risk.

passage:
Friday: Arnab's short film wins the college prize. He is buzzing. At the party, his friend Noor asks if he'll co-host the fest, edit her documentary and join a road trip to the beach, driving there and back the same night. "Yes, yes, yes!" he laughs. Everything feels easy.
Tuesday: The co-hosting rehearsal clashes with the documentary edit. He hasn't slept properly in three days. The road trip is Thursday, and he realises he would be driving eight hours overnight, exhausted.
Thursday: Arnab texts Noor: "Sorry, I said yes while I was floating. I can do the edit, not the co-hosting, and not the night drive. Driving that tired isn't safe." Noor replies with a thumbs-up. He sleeps for ten hours.

qa.q: How long would the overnight drive have been?
qa.a: Eight hours.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when he said yes three times at the party?
qa.a: He felt buzzing and elated after the prize, so everything felt easy and risks like a tired night drive did not register.

qa.q: What did Arnab do right on Thursday?
qa.a: He reassessed calmly, kept one commitment, and cancelled the co-hosting and the unsafe night drive, explaining honestly.

qa.q: How might Noor see Arnab's change of plan?
qa.a: She accepts it easily with a thumbs-up, probably glad he was honest rather than letting her down at the last minute.

grounding: A young adult in a great mood underestimates a risk and overcommits, then reconsiders when calmer.

passage: Pradeep, you have the face of someone who got good news and said yes to everything. I know that face. At twenty-one, your Sonali bua got her first job letter, and the same evening my college friends asked me to lead a trek up the ghats in the middle of the monsoon. I said yes before they finished the sentence. I also said yes to organising my cousin's engagement and to teaching a weekend class. In that happy haze, rain looked romantic, not dangerous. It was my father who asked quietly, "Have you heard the landslide warning on the radio?" I hadn't. We moved the trek to October. That very week, a road on that route was closed by a landslide. Joy is a lovely feeling, beta, but a poor judge of risk.

qa.q: When did they move the trek to?
qa.a: October.

qa.q: Why did young Sonali say yes before her friends finished the sentence?
qa.a: She was joyful after her first job letter, and in that happy haze the monsoon rain looked romantic rather than dangerous.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Her father's quiet question about the landslide warning, which made her check the risk and move the trek.

qa.q: How might Sonali's father have felt watching her say yes to everything?
qa.a: He was probably happy for her but quietly worried, which is why he asked about the warning instead of scolding.

grounding: An elder recalls how a great mood made her underestimate the risk of a monsoon trek and say yes to too much.

passage:
On New Year's Eve, an hour before midnight, Suraj got the email: internship accepted. He whooped so loudly the neighbours cheered.
In the next forty minutes, riding that high, he said yes to everything. Yes, he'd run the cultural fest's stage. Yes, he'd join Rohit's hackathon team. Yes, he'd help his cousin shift flats on the 6th. Yes, he'd tutor two juniors for their tests.
"All in the first week of January?" Damini asked, looking at his calendar. "That's also when your own mid-sems start."
"It'll be fine! I'm unstoppable this week." He could only picture it going well: the stage lights, the winning demo, grateful juniors.
Damini pointed at the 6th, where four things now overlapped. "Ask me again tomorrow morning, when you're just normal happy."

qa.q: What email did Suraj get an hour before midnight?
qa.a: That his internship was accepted.

qa.q: Why does saying yes to everything feel safe to Suraj?
qa.a: He is so joyful and excited that his mind only shows him things going well, so the clashes and his own mid-sems seem small.

qa.q: What is wise about Damini's suggestion?
qa.a: Deciding again the next morning, in a calmer mood, would let Suraj see the overlap on the 6th and the risk to his exams more clearly.

qa.q: How might Rohit and the juniors be affected if Suraj overcommits?
qa.a: They might be let down if he can't show up or prepare properly, even though he meant every yes.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a great mood underestimating risks and saying yes to too much.
